newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel seen immune to Southeast Asia forex turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Israel seen immune to Southeast Asia forex turmoil.

text.p: Currency turmoil plaguing Southeast Asian countries is unlikely to spread to Israel despite the shekel's short-lived plunge last month, analysts say.

The fact that Israel's economy relies more heavily on domestic investment and capital inflows are more stable, help its currency to shrug off the type of jitters which have hit other emerging markets recently, they said.
"The risk of global currency turmoil spreading to Israel and undermining the economy is, in our view, low at the present time," U.S. brokerage Bear Stearns' said in a recent report.

"Prior to the recent surge of foreign investments, Israel's growth had been internally financed to a much greater degree than in most emerging markets. Political risk has been a constant deterrent to foreign investment."
For most of the past year the Israeli shekel, pegged to a basket of foreign currencies, has hugged the lower limit or strong side of its trading band, sparking calls for a devaluation.
Last month the central bank widened the upper limit, or weak side, of the band, creating the potential for a sharp depreciation.
Within a few days the Israeli currency weakened by five percent, reaching 3.59 shekels to the dollar. The shekel at that point was 4.57 percent above the lower limit of the band.
But the currency has since recouped much of its losses and its rate against the basket is now only one percent above the lower limit. It is trading now at around 3.53 shekels against the dollar.
Many economists had predicted that the shekel's weakness was temporary, as big capital flows over the past year had supported the currency.

They were due in part to stepped-up foreign investment, but much was generated by Israelis taking advantage of lower overseas interest rates to borrow foreign currency and converting it cheaply into shekels, they said.
"With plentiful new opportunities for foreign investment and favourable treatment of risk capital, we expect continued healthy capital inflows," Bear Stearns said.
The report noted that favourable treatment for risk capital -- including tax exemptions or reductions for start-ups -- has made Israel a "high-tech hotbed".
"Most of the capital inflows I would characterise as long term," Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Sold Financial Markets said.
"It's Intel, Motorola and Volkswagen investing here. It's not, 'I'm here for a few days and pulling out,'" Katz said.
He predicted that capital inflows this year would rise about 35 percent to about $3 billion.
Katz noted another major difference between Israel and many Southeast Asian countries -- they tend to have much higher current account deficits.
Israel's Treasury forecast the deficit in 1997 will fall to 3.6 percent of gross domestic product from 5.6 percent in 1996.
Also, many emerging markets have managed exchange rate regimes with little room for fluctuations. The shekel's wide band would allow for a sharp depreciation if market forces so desired.
